title: Buffer Zones
hook: Running at full capacity feels efficient right up until one client pays late.
statement: Build slack into your plans so normal surprises don't turn into crises.
explainer: Averages hide the spikes. A business sized exactly for an average month breaks on a bad one. A buffer turns a crisis back into an inconvenience.
sop: Find where demand swings most: cash, staff hours, calendar, inbox.
Work out your Capacity and Avg Demand for that area.
Add a 10 to 20% buffer on top of average demand.
Decide ahead of time what counts as a reason to use it.
Review quarterly: too small, too big, or just right.
equation_example: Capacity is 100 hours, Avg Demand is 80. 100 - 80 = 20 hours of buffer. Higher means room to absorb a spike. Near zero or negative means any normal bump becomes an emergency.
question: Name the one place in your business running too tight to absorb a bad week.
closing_statement: Room to absorb shocks beats running at full tilt.
caption:
